references.text: Jesus himself explains what he means by this food: to do the will of the Father and complete his work. [ref:Joh 4:34|John 4:34] expands on the mysterious statement in verse 32.
Jesus speaks about food that does not perish but lasts for eternal life. [ref:Joh 6:27|John 6:27] uses the same motif of spiritual food versus physical food.
Jesus speaks of the true bread from heaven that gives life to the world. [ref:Joh 6:32-33|John 6:32-33] expands on the theme of heavenly nourishment that the disciples do not understand.

Moses reminds the people that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the Lord. [ref:5 Mos 8:3|Deuteronomy 8:3] establishes the foundation that God's will is a deeper nourishment than physical food.
Job says he has esteemed the words from God's mouth more than his daily bread. [ref:Job 23:12|Job 23:12] shows the same prioritization of God's will over physical sustenance.
The disciples had just asked Jesus to eat, and [ref:Joh 4:31|John 4:31] provides the immediate context for Jesus' answer about a food they do not know.
The disciples' reaction in [ref:Joh 4:33|John 4:33] shows that they misunderstand Jesus literally, a recurring theme in the Gospel of John where spiritual truths are understood on an earthly level.

God's invitation to come and eat and drink what truly satisfies points toward spiritual nourishment. [ref:Jes 55:1-2|Isaiah 55:1-2] uses food and drink metaphors for the life-giving power of God's word.

In his high priestly prayer, Jesus says he has glorified the Father by completing the work given to him. [ref:Joh 17:4|John 17:4] shows that Jesus' "food" – doing the Father's will – was his life mission.
Jesus does not seek his own will but the will of the one who sent him. [ref:Joh 5:30|John 5:30] emphasizes that Jesus' deepest driving force and nourishment is to do the Father's will.
